title: Establishing the pillars for building a safety culture
description: An example of a pillar-based model is the approach comprising: the mental and spiritual pillar (awareness), the legal and organisational pillar (procedures).

blocks.text: Here are the main objectives of establishing the pillars of safety culture that guide us in our collaboration with you:

An example of a pillar-based model is the approach comprising: the mental and spiritual pillar (awareness), the legal and organisational pillar (procedures) and the material pillar (infrastructure), which enables comprehensive safety management.

items: Ensuring consistency and commitment: The ‘leadership’ or ‘management commitment’ pillar ensures that safety is not merely the responsibility of the health and safety department, but a value upheld by senior management, which motivates employees.

Reducing accidents and risks: Through the standardisation of activities (pillars such as audits and hazard reporting), the company is better able to identify and eliminate risks, thereby reducing fatal and serious accidents.

Changing employee mindset: The mental and spiritual pillar helps shift employees’ mindset from “I must follow the rules” to “I want to be safe”, which builds a culture of trust and shared responsibility.
Fostering positive behaviours (BBS): The pillars help implement a behaviour-based safety (BBS) approach, rewarding safe behaviours and teaching root cause analysis rather than simply assigning blame.
Cost optimisation and business continuity: A strong safety culture, supported by organisational pillars, reduces sick leave, insurance costs and production downtime.
Creating a competitive advantage: Organisations with a strong safety culture are perceived as more reliable business partners, which makes it easier to attract contractors.
